*[One Piece](One_Piece "One Piece")* is a Japanese [media franchise](Media_franchise "Media franchise") created by [Eiichirō Oda](Eiichir%C5%8D_Oda "Eiichirō Oda") in 1997. The [initial manga](One_Piece "One Piece"), written and illustrated by [Eiichirō Oda](Eiichir%C5%8D_Oda "Eiichirō Oda"), has been serialized in <Shueisha>'s *[Weekly Shōnen Jump](Weekly_Sh%C5%8Dnen_Jump "Weekly Shōnen Jump")* magazine since July 22, 1997, and has been collected into 105 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes. As of March 2023, the manga has sold over 510 million copies worldwide, making it the [best-selling manga series](List_of_best-selling_manga "List of best-selling manga") in history. It became the best-selling manga for the eleventh consecutive year in 2018.

The manga has been adapted into a festival film produced by [Production I.G](Production_I.G "Production I.G") in 1998, an [anime](Anime "Anime") [series](One_Piece_(TV_series) "One Piece (TV series)") produced by [Toei Animation](Toei_Animation "Toei Animation"), which began broadcasting in Japan in 1999, and a [live-action series](One_Piece_(2023_TV_series) "One Piece (2023 TV series)") produced by Tomorrow Studios, released by <Netflix> in 2023. Additionally, Toei has developed 13 animated feature films, [original video animations](Original_video_animation "Original video animation"), and 13 television specials. Several companies have developed various types of merchandise like trading card games and [numerous video games](List_of_One_Piece_video_games "List of One Piece video games"). In addition, there has been other material released based on the franchise, such as [spin-off manga](Spin-off_(media) "Spin-off (media)"), [light novels](Light_novel "Light novel"), [anime comics](Film_comic "Film comic"), [artbooks](Artbook "Artbook"), [soundtracks](Soundtrack "Soundtrack"), [databooks](Guide_book "Guide book"), [magazines](Magazines "Magazines"), [attractions](Attractions "Attractions"), and [theatrical plays](Play_(theatre) "Play (theatre)").

*[One Piece](One_Piece "One Piece")* is a Japanese [media franchise](Media_franchise "Media franchise") created by [Eiichirō Oda](Eiichir%C5%8D_Oda "Eiichirō Oda") in 1997. The [initial manga](One_Piece "One Piece"), written and illustrated by [Eiichirō Oda](Eiichir%C5%8D_Oda "Eiichirō Oda"), has been serialized in <Shueisha>'s *[Weekly Shōnen Jump](Weekly_Sh%C5%8Dnen_Jump "Weekly Shōnen Jump")* magazine since July 22, 1997, and has been collected into 105 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes. As of March 2023, the manga has sold over 510 million copies worldwide, making it the [best-selling manga series](List_of_best-selling_manga "List of best-selling manga") in history. It became the best-selling manga for the eleventh consecutive year in 2018.

The manga has been adapted into a festival film produced by [Production I.G](Production_I.G "Production I.G") in 1998, an [anime](Anime "Anime") [series](One_Piece_(TV_series) "One Piece (TV series)") produced by [Toei Animation](Toei_Animation "Toei Animation"), which began broadcasting in Japan in 1999, and a [live-action series](One_Piece_(2023_TV_series) "One Piece (2023 TV series)") produced by Tomorrow Studios, released by <Netflix> in 2023. Additionally, Toei has developed 13 animated feature films, [original video animations](Original_video_animation "Original video animation"), and 13 television specials. Several companies have developed various types of merchandise like trading card games and [numerous video games](List_of_One_Piece_video_games "List of One Piece video games"). In addition, there has been other material released based on the franchise, such as [spin-off manga](Spin-off_(media) "Spin-off (media)"), [light novels](Light_novel "Light novel"), [anime comics](Film_comic "Film comic"), [artbooks](Artbook "Artbook"), [soundtracks](Soundtrack "Soundtrack"), [databooks](Guide_book "Guide book"), [magazines](Magazines "Magazines"), [attractions](Attractions "Attractions"), and [theatrical plays](Play_(theatre) "Play (theatre)").

content:
Based on my research, I found information about One Piece light novel adaptations. Here's what I discovered:

## Yes, One Piece Has Light Novel Adaptations

According to Wikipedia's "List of One Piece media," **One Piece has 29 published novels** in total. These include both original light novels and film/TV special adaptations.

### Original One Piece Light Novels

The original light novel adaptations (not based on films) include:

1. **One Piece: Loguetown Arc** (July 17, 2000) - Featured deleted scenes from the Loguetown Arc that were incorporated into the anime
2. **One Piece: The Legend of Thousand Year Dragon** (December 25, 2001)
3. **One Piece novel: Straw Hat Stories** (November 2, 2017) - By Tomohito Ohsaki
4. **One Piece novel A** (2018) - Two volumes focusing on the formation of the Spade Pirates, adapted into a manga by Boichi
5. **One Piece novel Law** (April 3, 2020) - By Akinari Sakagami
6. **One Piece novel HEROINES** (June 4, 2021) - By Jun Esaka

### Film and TV Special Novelizations

The majority of the 29 novels are adaptations of One Piece films and TV specials, including:
- One Piece: Defeat Him! The Pirate Ganzack (OVA - 1999)
- One Piece Film: Strong World (2009)
- One Piece Film: Z (2012)
- One Piece Film: Gold (2016)
- One Piece: Stampede (2019)
- One Piece Film: Red (2022)
- And several other film adaptations

### Western Light Novels (English)

There were also some Western-published light novels by Scholastic based on the 4Kids anime version:
- **King Of The Pirates** (2007) - By Micheal Anthony Steele
- **The Circus Comes To Town** (2007) - By Howie Dewin
- **Tall Tales** (2007)
- **Pirate Attack** (2007)
- **Recipe For Disaster** (2007)

So in summary, **One Piece does have light novel adaptations** with 29 total published novels, consisting of a mix of original stories and film/TV special novelizations.

Duke Togo has a very quiet personality and will only talk when he needs to, he shows very little to no emotion when carrying out an [assassination](Assassination "Assassination") and is willing to kill anyone who will threaten to expose him. He accepts many different assassination jobs, from anyone who can afford his services. From simply shooting a violin string to taking out powerful organized crime bosses and political figures, these killings have often attracted retaliations against Golgo 13, even at one stage having both the FBI, CIA, and even the United States military out to kill him, causing Togo to always have to watch his own back and pay attention to his surroundings in order to stop other assassins and contract killers employed to kill him in often creative ways. Golgo 13 also employs many different people himself to assist him in his assassination jobs, such as in providing extra information on his targets to modifying his weapons, vehicles, and gadgets.

The name "Golgo 13" is a reference to the [death of Jesus Christ](Death_of_Jesus_Christ "Death of Jesus Christ"). *Golgo* is short for <Golgotha>, the place of <Jesus>' crucifixion, while the [number 13](13_(number) "13 (number)") is considered an unlucky number.[[3]](Golgo_13#cite_note-3) Also, Golgo 13's logo is a skeleton wearing a [crown of thorns](Crown_of_thorns "Crown of thorns").

Duke Togo's past is a mystery. Although his Asian appearance suggests that he may be of Japanese origin, many of Golgo 13's stories have presented different speculations about his true identity while presenting contradictory information, leaving the audience uncertain which information is true. It is known that he may be the biological father of many different children all over the world from the many sexual encounters he has had with women throughout the series, such as a four-year-old son named Joey from ex-[Provisional Irish Republican Army](Provisional_Irish_Republican_Army "Provisional Irish Republican Army") fighter Catherine McCall.[[4]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Episode_26-4)[[5]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Episode_48-5)

With respect to the character's age, a large number of stories are dated as they are centered around current events of the time. However, Golgo 13's age [has not increased significantly](Floating_timeline "Floating timeline") to account for these events. He has also suffered multiple injuries throughout the series, leaving many different scars on his body.[[6]](Golgo_13#cite_note-DV-6)

## Production

Early on, [Takao Saito](Takao_Saito "Takao Saito") developed a system where he created the page layout based on a script written by the editorial department. He also inked the main characters' faces, while assistants provided the backgrounds and other elements. He did extensive research to provide accuracy, especially when the plot dealt with technology.[[7]](Golgo_13#cite_note-7) [Kazuo Koike](Kazuo_Koike "Kazuo Koike") was one of the writers on the series in the beginning.[[8]](Golgo_13#cite_note-8)[[9]](Golgo_13#cite_note-9) Author [Yoichi Funado](Yoichi_Funado "Yoichi Funado") wrote approximately 30 stories for *Golgo 13*, three of which he later novelized.[[10]](Golgo_13#cite_note-10) [Takashi Nagasaki](Takashi_Nagasaki "Takashi Nagasaki") was Saito's editor on the series in the mid-1980s, and later wrote two stories for the manga under the pen name "Keishi Edogawa".[[11]](Golgo_13#cite_note-11)

According to [Jason Thompson](Jason_Thompson_(writer) "Jason Thompson (writer)"), several *Golgo 13* stories have not been reprinted for being "offensive or libelous". Thompson lists one from 1986 because of complaints from the [Iranian embassy in Japan](Embassy_of_Iran%2C_Tokyo "Embassy of Iran, Tokyo"), another from 1988 about [money laundering](Money_laundering "Money laundering") in the Vatican, and one from 1989 about a Hollywood actor blackmailed when someone discovers he has [AIDS](HIV/AIDS "HIV/AIDS").[[12]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Thompson-12)

In 2013, Saito stated that because he often worried about his manga being cancelled, he had an ending planned out that even included the panel layout. He said he had no idea when *Golgo 13* would end, claiming "The manga has continued so long that it is no longer the property of the author; it belongs to the readers."[[13]](Golgo_13#cite_note-13) Two years later, *[Big Comic](Big_Comic "Big Comic")*'s fourth issue of 2015 announced that the series was "heading towards its conclusion."[[14]](Golgo_13#cite_note-14)

Due to difficulties that arose from the restrictions implemented by the government to combat the [COVID-19 pandemic in Japan](COVID-19_pandemic_in_Japan "COVID-19 pandemic in Japan"), *Golgo 13* began its first hiatus in its 52-year history in May 2020.[[15]](Golgo_13#cite_note-15) It returned on July 7, 2020.[[16]](Golgo_13#cite_note-16)

Saito died of [pancreatic cancer](Pancreatic_cancer "Pancreatic cancer") at 84 on September 24, 2021.[[17]](Golgo_13#cite_note-17)[[18]](Golgo_13#cite_note-18) According to <Shogakukan>, Saito said before his death that he wanted the manga to continue on without him. The Saito Production group of manga creators continues its publication with the assistance of *Big Comic*'s editorial department.[[19]](Golgo_13#cite_note-19)

## Media

### Manga

Main article: [List of *Golgo 13* chapters](List_of_Golgo_13_chapters "List of Golgo 13 chapters")

Written and illustrated by [Takao Saito](Takao_Saito "Takao Saito"), *Golgo 13* has been serialized in the monthly manga magazine *[Big Comic](Big_Comic "Big Comic")* since its January 1969 issue, published in October 1968.[[20]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Golgo_13_Start-20) The chapters have been collected into *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes by <Shogakukan> and [Leed Publishing](Leed_Publishing "Leed Publishing"), a spinoff of the author's own Saito Production,[[12]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Thompson-12) since June 21, 1973.[[21]](Golgo_13#cite_note-21) As of July 2023, 209 volumes of the *tankōbon* edition have been published,[[22]](Golgo_13#cite_note-22) while the *[bunkoban](Bunkoban "Bunkoban")* edition has 167 volumes.[[23]](Golgo_13#cite_note-23)

In 1986, Leed Publishing released four *Golgo 13* stories translated by Patrick Connolly: "Into the Wolves' Lair", "Galinpero", "The Ice Lake Hit" and "The Ivory Connection".[[12]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Thompson-12)[[24]](Golgo_13#cite_note-24)

In 1989 and 1990, Leed and [Vic Tokai](Vic_Tokai "Vic Tokai") published two further *Golgo 13* comic books, "The Impossible Hit" and "The Border Hopper", as part of the promotion for two *Golgo 13* video games.[[12]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Thompson-12) The comics were released to the US public via a mail-in offer with the purchase of the games and were later even found packaged with the video games. Each issue contained one complete story and had nothing to do with the storylines of the video games themselves.

In 1991, Leed Publishing and [Viz Media](Viz_Media "Viz Media") published *The Professional: Golgo 13*, a three-part mini-series.[[12]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Thompson-12) *The Professional* was a re-printing of "The Argentine Tiger", a story where Golgo is hired by the British Government to assassinate the reportedly dead ex-president of Argentina [Juan Perón](Juan_Per%C3%B3n "Juan Perón").

In 2006, *Golgo 13* was brought back by Viz as part of their Viz Signature collection. The stories are picked from the forty-year history of the manga, and do not necessarily represent the original's order of publication. A total of thirteen volumes were published, with the thirteenth volume being published on February 19, 2008. Each volume ends with an editorial commentary on *Golgo 13* as a cultural phenomenon in Japan.[[6]](Golgo_13#cite_note-DV-6)

A spin-off manga titled *Gunsmith Dave* (銃器職人・デイブ) and focusing on the character Dave McCartney began serialization in the August special issue of *Big Comic* on July 17, 2021.[[25]](Golgo_13#cite_note-25) The spin-off ended its "first season" on May 17, 2022.[[26]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Third-spin-off-26) Saito and Saito Production are credited with creating the manga.[[27]](Golgo_13#cite_note-27)

A second spin-off, *Golgo Camp* (ゴルゴCAMP) created by Yukio Miyama, was launched on Shogakukan's *Manga One* app on August 28, 2021.[[28]](Golgo_13#cite_note-28) It is a gag comedy and follows Golgo 13 at a modern-day campsite.[[29]](Golgo_13#cite_note-29)

A third spin-off, *G no Idenshi: Shōjo Fanette* (Gの遺伝子 少女ファネット), began serialization in the August issue of *Big Comic Zōkan* on July 15, 2022.[[26]](Golgo_13#cite_note-Third-spin-off-26) It focuses on the French junior high school student Fanette, who has Golgo's genes.[[30]](Golgo_13#cite_note-30)

### Live action

Main articles: [*Golgo 13* (film)](Golgo_13_(film) "Golgo 13 (film)") and [*Golgo 13: Assignment Kowloon*](Golgo_13%3A_Assignment_Kowloon "Golgo 13: Assignment Kowloon")

[Toei Company](Toei_Company "Toei Company") produced a live-action film simply titled *Golgo 13* in 1973, directed by [Junya Sato](Junya_Sato "Junya Sato") and starring [Ken Takakura](Ken_Takakura "Ken Takakura") as Duke Togo and [Pouri Banayi](Pouri_Banayi "Pouri Banayi") as Catherine Morton. It was filmed entirely in the [Imperial State of Iran](Pahlavi_dynasty "Pahlavi dynasty") with an entirely [Persian](Persian_people "Persian people") supporting cast. It was followed by *[Golgo 13: Assignment Kowloon](Golgo_13%3A_Assignment_Kowloon "Golgo 13: Assignment Kowloon")* in 1977, directed by Yukio Noda, which replaced Takakura with [Sonny Chiba](Sonny_Chiba "Sonny Chiba"). In 2011, production company Davis Film obtained the American film rights to *Golgo*.[[31]](Golgo_13#cite_note-31)

The episodes of *[Golgo 13](Golgo_13 "Golgo 13")* are based on the manga of the same name, which had aired in Spring 2008, but were re-imagined to fit current real-world synchronism.[[1]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-1) The first episode aired in Japanese on April 11, 2008[[2]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-2)[[3]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-3) with Japanese television actor [Hiroshi Tachi](Hiroshi_Tachi "Hiroshi Tachi") playing the role of Duke Togo.[[4]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-4)[[5]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-AS-5) The series is animated by The Answer Studio Co., Ltd.,[[5]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-AS-5)[[6]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-Staff_and_Cast-6) and directed by Shunji Oga,[[7]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-7) who also did some storyboard work based on the *Golgo 13* franchise.

The episodes are based on Duke Togo aka Golgo 13, an internationally known mercenary assassin, who is known by law enforcement agencies, criminals, terrorists and other factions around the world. He is notorious around the world as he is hired by many persons ranging from individuals, who can afford to hire him for an assignment, to foreign governments and secret organizations. The show details the various tasks that he undertakes and his encounters with various people.

The opening theme, *Take The Wave*, was performed by Naifu with the second opening theme *So faraway* performed by Pinc Inc[[6]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-Staff_and_Cast-6)[[8]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-8) played beginning from episode 26 with the exception of episode 19 and 21 since it used *Take The Wave* as its opening theme. For episodes 1 to 12, the ending theme song *Garasu no Haiwei* or Glass Highway was performed by [doa](Doa_(Japanese_band) "Doa (Japanese band)"), released in their album *Prime Garden* on November 19, 2008.[[9]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-9) The second ending theme song *Yume no Hitotsu* was performed by [GARNET CROW](Garnet_Crow "Garnet Crow") with their single released on August 13, 2008.[[10]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-10) The third ending song *Sono Hohoemi Yo Eien ni* is performed by [Aiko Kitahara](Aiko_Kitahara "Aiko Kitahara") from episodes 26 to 38. It was released a single on November 5, 2008.[[11]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-11) The fourth and final ending theme, "Mou Kimi wo Hitori ni Sasenai", was performed by [U-KA Saegusa in DB](U-ka_Saegusa_in_dB "U-ka Saegusa in dB") with the single released on February 25, 2009.[[12]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-12)

Golgo 13 has already been released for the DVD. Volume 1 of the series has been released to the public on June 26, 2009.[[13]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-13) Volume 2 was released on July 24, 2009.[[14]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-14) Volume 3 has already been released on August 25, 2009.[[15]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-15) Volume 4 was released on September 25, 2009.[[16]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-16)

Aside from DVD releases, the show is also released on the [UMD](Universal_Media_Disc "Universal Media Disc") with a few select episodes taken from the series released publicly as *Golgo 13: Best Selection*.[[17]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-Best_Selection-17) The first volume, released on June 26, 2009, includes episodes 15, 32, 39 and 49.[[17]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-Best_Selection-17)[[18]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-18) The second volume was released on July 24, 2009 with episodes 14, 26, 33 and 34.[[17]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-Best_Selection-17)[[19]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-19) The third volume was released on August 25, 2009.[[20]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-20)

The series has been licensed in North America by [Sentai Filmworks](Sentai_Filmworks "Sentai Filmworks"), and distributed by [Section23 Films](Section23_Films "Section23 Films"). The first DVD set was released on July 13, 2010, with an English dub.[[21]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-21) The second set was released on September 14, 2010.[[22]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-22) The English dub is currently streaming on the [Anime Network](Anime_Network "Anime Network").[[23]](List_of_Golgo_13_episodes#cite_note-23)

**Kenji Harada** (原田建司, *Harada Kenji*, February 8, 1944 – April 22, 2015) better known by his pseudonym **Yoichi Funado** (船戸与一, *Funado Yoichi*) was a [Japanese](Japanese_people "Japanese people") writer of [adventure fiction](Adventure_fiction "Adventure fiction").[[1]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-Yoichi-1)

## Biography

Funado was born as Kenji Harada on February 8, 1944. During his student days, he traveled to <Alaska>. He graduated from [Waseda University](Waseda_University "Waseda University").[[1]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-Yoichi-1) Funado wrote approximately 30 stories for the [manga](Manga "Manga") series *[Golgo 13](Golgo_13 "Golgo 13")*, three of which he later novelized in 2011.[[2]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-2)

Funado made his debut as an [adventure novel writer](Adventure_fiction "Adventure fiction") in 1979.[[1]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-Yoichi-1) After writing some prize-winning adventure novels, in 2000 he won the [Naoki Prize](Naoki_Prize "Naoki Prize") for his novel *May in the Valley of the Rainbow*.[[1]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-Yoichi-1)[[3]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-YF-3) In February 2015, he published the last volume of his nine-volume novel series on the history of <Manchukuo>.

Funado died of [thymic cancer](Thymic_carcinoma "Thymic carcinoma") on April 22, 2015, in Suginami, Tokyo.[[1]](Yoichi_Funado#cite_note-Yoichi-1)

The first volume was released on June 18, 1994.[[21]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Vol_1-24) On October 18, 2021, the series reached one hundred volumes;[[22]](Case_Closed#cite_note-25) *[One Piece](One_Piece "One Piece")* author, [Eiichiro Oda](Eiichiro_Oda "Eiichiro Oda"), whose series achieved the same feat a month before, sent congratulations to Aoyama.[[23]](Case_Closed#cite_note-26) As of April 12, 2023, 103 volumes have been published.[[24]](Case_Closed#cite_note-27)

[Viz Media](Viz_Media "Viz Media") announced its acquisition of the series for North America on June 1, 2004.[[25]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Viz_announce-28) Following Funimation's localization, Viz released the series as *Case Closed* and took their character names to keep consistency between the two media.[[26]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Viz_rename-29) Viz Media released the first volume in September 2004 and began releasing digital editions in 2013.[[27]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Viz_1-30)[[28]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Digital_Viz_1-31) On May 9, 2023, Viz Media launched their *Viz Manga* digital manga service, with the series' chapters receiving simultaneous English publication in North America as they are released in Japan.[[29]](Case_Closed#cite_note-32)[[30]](Case_Closed#cite_note-33) [Gollancz](Victor_Gollancz_Ltd "Victor Gollancz Ltd") licensed and distributed 15 of Viz Media's volumes in the United Kingdom before ceasing publication of manga. (Viz Media has since re-released them).[[31]](Case_Closed#cite_note-34) In 2014 [Shogakukan Asia](Shogakukan_Asia "Shogakukan Asia") began its own English localization of the series for Singapore and other Southeast Asian countries as *Detective Conan*.[[32]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Singapore_manga-35) Laura Thornton of <CBR.com>, citing the common Japanese ownership in both Shogakukan Asia and Viz, described the Singapore version as, compared to the Viz one, "completely identical, word-for-word, even -- save for the names and the *Detective Conan* logo".[[33]](Case_Closed#cite_note-ThorntonLaura-36)

The manga has also been localized in other regions such as China, France, Germany and Indonesia.[[34]](Case_Closed#cite_note-37)[[35]](Case_Closed#cite_note-38)[[36]](Case_Closed#cite_note-39)[[37]](Case_Closed#cite_note-40) Localizations in Scandinavia ceased one by one, Finland being the last in 2013, when the publisher shut down the entire manga division.[[38]](Case_Closed#cite_note-41)[[39]](Case_Closed#cite_note-42)[[40]](Case_Closed#cite_note-43)[[41]](Case_Closed#cite_note-44)

### Spin-offs

Main articles: [*Case Closed: The Culprit Hanzawa*](Case_Closed%3A_The_Culprit_Hanzawa "Case Closed: The Culprit Hanzawa"), [*Case Closed: Zero's Tea Time*](Case_Closed%3A_Zero's_Tea_Time "Case Closed: Zero's Tea Time"), and [*Detective Conan: Police Academy Arc*](Detective_Conan%3A_Police_Academy_Arc "Detective Conan: Police Academy Arc")

Gosho Aoyama's assistants have written an [anthology](Anthology "Anthology") series of *Case Closed* which are released irregularly.[[42]](Case_Closed#cite_note-Short_1-45)[[43]](Case_Closed#cite_note-46)

A [spin-off](Spin-off_(media) "Spin-off (media)") manga series, titled *Case Closed: The Culprit Hanzawa*, by Mayuko Kanba, began in the July 2017 issue of <Shogakukan>'s *[Shōnen Sunday S](Sh%C5%8Dnen_Sunday_S "Shōnen Sunday S")*, released on May 25, 2017.[[44]](Case_Closed#cite_note-47)

Another spin-off manga series, illustrated by Takahiro Arai with supervision by Aoyama, titled *Case Closed: Zero's Tea Time* started in issue #24 of *Weekly Shōnen Sunday* on May 9, 2018. The story centers on the agent [Toru Amuro/Rei Furuya](List_of_Case_Closed_characters#Rei_Furuya "List of Case Closed characters").[[45]](Case_Closed#cite_note-48) New chapters of the manga are only published when *Case Closed* is on hiatus.

Another spin-off manga series by Arai, titled *Detective Conan: Police Academy Arc – Wild Police Story*, was serialized in *Weekly Shōnen Sunday* from October 2, 2019, to November 18, 2020. Spanning 13 chapters, it again focuses on Amuro/Furuya during his years in the police academy with his colleagues.[[46]](Case_Closed#cite_note-49)[[47]](Case_Closed#cite_note-50)[[48]](Case_Closed#cite_note-51)

***Dragon Ball*** ([Japanese](Japanese_language "Japanese language"): ドラゴンボール, [Hepburn](Hepburn_romanization "Hepburn romanization"): *Doragon Bōru*) is a Japanese [media franchise](Media_franchise "Media franchise") created by [Akira Toriyama](Akira_Toriyama "Akira Toriyama") in 1984. The [initial manga](Dragon_Ball_(manga) "Dragon Ball (manga)"), written and illustrated by Toriyama, was serialized in *[Weekly Shōnen Jump](Weekly_Sh%C5%8Dnen_Jump "Weekly Shōnen Jump")* from 1984 to 1995, with the 519 individual chapters collected into 42 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes by its publisher <Shueisha>. *Dragon Ball* was originally inspired by the classical 16th-century Chinese novel *[Journey to the West](Journey_to_the_West "Journey to the West")*, combined with elements of [Hong Kong martial arts films](Hong_Kong_martial_arts_films "Hong Kong martial arts films"). *Dragon Ball* characters also use a variety of [East Asian martial arts](List_of_martial_arts#Asia "List of martial arts") styles, including [karate](Karate "Karate")[[1]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-1)[[2]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-:1-3) and [Wing Chun](Wing_Chun "Wing Chun") ([kung fu](Kung_fu_(term) "Kung fu (term)")).[[2]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-:0-2)[[3]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-:1-3)[[4]](Dragon_Ball#cite_note-4) The series follows the adventures of protagonist [Son Goku](Goku "Goku") from his childhood through adulthood as he trains in martial arts. He spends his childhood far from civilization until he meets a teen girl named <Bulma>, who encourages him to join her quest in exploring the world in search of the seven orbs known as the Dragon Balls, which summon a wish-granting dragon when gathered. Along his journey, Goku makes several other friends, becomes a family man, discovers his alien heritage, and battles a wide variety of villains, many of whom also seek the Dragon Balls.

Toriyama's [manga](Manga "Manga") was adapted and divided into two [anime](Anime "Anime") series produced by [Toei Animation](Toei_Animation "Toei Animation"): *[Dragon Ball](Dragon_Ball_(TV_series) "Dragon Ball (TV series)")* and *[Dragon Ball Z](Dragon_Ball_Z "Dragon Ball Z")*, which together were broadcast in Japan from 1986 to 1996. From 2009 to 2015, a revised version of *Dragon Ball Z* aired in Japan under the title *Dragon Ball Kai*, as a recut that follows the manga's story more faithfully by removing most of the material featured exclusively in the anime. Based on my search of Wikipedia, I found detailed information about Dragon Ball companion books. Here's what I discovered:

## Dragon Ball Light Novel Adaptations

**Dragon Ball does not have traditional light novel adaptations.** However, it has numerous **companion books** (guidebooks), which are different from light novels in that they are non-fiction reference materials rather than fictional narrative works.

## Dragon Ball Companion Books

The Dragon Ball franchise has several companion book series:

### 1. **Daizenshuu (大全集) Series**
- **7 hardback main volumes + 3 supplemental softcover volumes**
- Published 1995
- Covers the manga, first two anime series (Dragon Ball and Dragon Ball Z), and theatrical films
- **Volume 1: "Dragon Ball: The Complete Illustrations"** - Only one released in English by Viz Media (2008)
  - Contains all 264 colored illustrations by Akira Toriyama for Weekly Shōnen Jump covers
  - Includes 42 tankōbon covers
  - Features an interview with Toriyama
- Remaining volumes never released in English, now out of print in Japan

### 2. **Chōzenshū (超全集) Series**
- **4 volumes** released February-May 2013
- Condensed versions of Daizenshuu with updated information

### 3. **Dragon Ball GT Perfect Files**
- **2 volumes** released May/December 1997 (re-released April 2006)
- Published by Shueisha's Jump Comics Selection imprint
- Still in print

### 4. **2003-2004 Guidebooks**
- Dragon Ball Landmark, Dragon Ball Forever (manga coverage)
- Dragon Ball: Tenkaichi Densetsu, Dragon Ball Z: Son Goku Densetsu (anime coverage)
- Includes new interviews and unpublished artwork

### 5. **Post-Kai Guidebooks**
- Dragon Ball: Super Exciting Guide (2009) - 2 volumes
- Dragon Ball: Extreme Battle Collection (2010) - 2 volumes
- Dragon Ball: Anime Illustrations Guide – The Golden Warrior (2010)

These companion books are reference works, not light novel adaptations. The manga itself is the source material that spawned the entire franchise, including anime, films, and video games, but not light novels.

***Doraemon*** (ドラえもん) is a Japanese [manga](Manga "Manga") series written and illustrated by [Fujiko F. Fujio](Fujiko_F._Fujio "Fujiko F. Fujio"). The manga was first serialized in December 1969. Its chapters were collected in 45 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes published by <Shogakukan> from 1974 to 1996. The story revolves around an earless robotic cat named [Doraemon](Doraemon_(character) "Doraemon (character)"), who [travels back in time](Time_travel "Time travel") from the 22nd century to aid a boy named [Nobita Nobi](Nobita_Nobi "Nobita Nobi").

The manga spawned a [media franchise](Media_franchise "Media franchise"). Three anime TV series have been adapted in [1973](Doraemon_(1973_TV_series) "Doraemon (1973 TV series)"), [1979](Doraemon_(1979_TV_series) "Doraemon (1979 TV series)"), and [2005](Doraemon_(2005_TV_series) "Doraemon (2005 TV series)"). Additionally, [Shin-Ei Animation](Shin-Ei_Animation "Shin-Ei Animation") has produced [over forty animated films](List_of_Doraemon_films "List of Doraemon films"), including two 3D computer-animated films, all of which are distributed by <Toho>. Various types of merchandise and media have been developed, including [soundtrack albums](List_of_Doraemon_soundtrack_albums "List of Doraemon soundtrack albums"), [video games](List_of_Doraemon_video_games "List of Doraemon video games"), and musicals. The manga series was licensed for an English language release in North America, via [Amazon Kindle](Amazon_Kindle "Amazon Kindle"), by a collaboration of Fujiko F. Fujio Pro with [Voyager Japan](Voyager_Books "Voyager Books") and [AltJapan Co., Ltd.](AltJapan_Co.%2C_Ltd. "AltJapan Co., Ltd.") The anime series was licensed by [Disney](The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") for an English-language release in North America in 2014, and LUK International in [Europe, the Middle East and Africa](Europe%2C_the_Middle_East_and_Africa "Europe, the Middle East and Africa").

*Doraemon* was well-received by critics and became a hit in many Asian countries. It won numerous awards, including the [Japan Cartoonists Association Award](Japan_Cartoonists_Association_Award "Japan Cartoonists Association Award") in 1973 and 1994, the [Shogakukan Manga Award](Shogakukan_Manga_Award "Shogakukan Manga Award") for [children's manga](Children's_anime_and_manga "Children's anime and manga") in 1982, and the [Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize](Tezuka_Osamu_Cultural_Prize "Tezuka Osamu Cultural Prize") in 1997. By 2019, it has sold over 250 million copies

## Synopsis

See also: [List of *Doraemon* characters](List_of_Doraemon_characters "List of Doraemon characters")

[Nobita Nobi](Nobita_Nobi "Nobita Nobi") is a ten-year-old Japanese school boy, who is kind-hearted and honest, but also lazy, unlucky, weak, gets bad grades and is bad at sports. One day, a robot cat from the 22nd century named Doraemon is sent back to the past by Nobita's future grandchild, Sewashi Nobi, to take care of Nobita so that his descendants can have a better life. Doraemon has a four-dimensional pouch in which he stores tools, inventions, and gadgets from the future to aid Nobita whenever he is faced with a problem. Although Doraemon is a cat robot, he has a fear of mice because of an incident where robotic mice chewed off his ears. This is why Doraemon lost his original yellow color and turned blue, from sadness.

Nobita has three main friends: [Takeshi Goda](Takeshi_Goda "Takeshi Goda") (nicknamed Gian), [Suneo Honekawa](Suneo_Honekawa "Suneo Honekawa") (Gian's sidekick), and [Shizuka Minamoto](Shizuka_Minamoto "Shizuka Minamoto"), Nobita's best friend and love-interest. Gian is a strong, leading and domineering boy, but also loyal to his friends. Suneo is a wealthy and spoiled boy who uses his friendship with Gian to win the respect of other schoolmates. Shizuka is a gentle and kind girl who frequently plays with Nobita. Nobita has a crush on Shizuka; she is his prospective future wife (Nobita's future wife is initially Gian's younger sister). Although Gian and Suneo are Nobita's friends, they also typically bully and abuse him. Nobita normally responds by using Doraemon's gadgets to fight back against them, but Nobita has a tendency to get carried away with using the gadgets (or Gian and Suneo, if they steal it away), which typically results in unintended consequences for him and others.

In addition to Gian, Suneo, and Shizuka, Dorami and Hidetoshi Dekisugi (common name Dekisugi) are also recurring characters. Dorami is Doraemon's younger sister, and Dekisugi is a gifted student boy who as Shizuka's close friend, frequently attracts the jealousy of Nobita.

## Creation and conception

### Development and themes

*Doraemon* is written and illustrated by [Fujiko F. Fujio](Fujiko_Fujio "Fujiko Fujio"), the pen name of Japanese [manga artist](Manga_artist "Manga artist") Hiroshi Fujimoto.[[6]](Doraemon#cite_note-6)[[7]](Doraemon#cite_note-:25-7)[[8]](Doraemon#cite_note-Doraworld-8) According to Fujio, it was originally conceived following a series of three events: when searching for ideas for a new manga, he wished a machine existed that would come up with ideas for him, he tripped over his daughter's toy, and heard cats fighting in his neighborhood.[[9]](Doraemon#cite_note-:0-9) To set up the plot and characters, he inspired some elements from his earlier manga series, *[Obake no Q-Tarō](Obake_no_Q-Tar%C5%8D "Obake no Q-Tarō")*, which involve an *[obake](Obake "Obake")* living with humans, with a similar formula.[[10]](Doraemon#cite_note-:20-10) Fujio said that the idea for *Doraemon* came after "an accumulation of trial and error", during which he finally found the most suitable style of manga to him.[[11]](Doraemon#cite_note-11) Initially, the series achieved little success as *[gekiga](Gekiga "Gekiga")* was well-known at the time, and only became a hit after its adaptation into an anime TV series and multiple feature films.[[10]](Doraemon#cite_note-:20-10)

*Doraemon* is mainly aimed at children, so Fujio chose to create the character with a simple graphic style, based on shapes such as circles and ellipses.[[12]](Doraemon#cite_note-12) He used the same sequences of cartoons with regularity and continuity to enhance the reader's ease of understanding. In addition, blue, a characteristic color of Doraemon, was chosen as the main color in magazine publications, which used to have a yellow cover and red title.[[13]](Doraemon#cite_note-:30-13) Set in <Tokyo>, the manga reflected parts of Japan's society, such as the class system and the "ideal" of Japanese childhood.[[14]](Doraemon#cite_note-:4-14)[[15]](Doraemon#cite_note-15) Problems, if occur, were resolved in a way so as not to rely on violence and eroticism,[[16]](Doraemon#cite_note-16) and the stories were integrated with the concept of environmentalism.[[17]](Doraemon#cite_note-17) The manga also insisted on the ethical values of integrity, perseverance, courage, family and respect.[[18]](Doraemon#cite_note-18)

This list of *<Doraemon>* films features both feature-length and short films based on the [manga](Manga "Manga") and [anime](Anime "Anime") series *<Doraemon>*. Since 1980, all of these films to date have been released by <Toho>. Toho currently holds worldwide distribution and licensing rights for all of the films in the series.

At the [Japanese box office](Cinema_of_Japan "Cinema of Japan"), *Doraemon* had grossed more than ¥100 billion revenue and sold more than 100 million tickets by 2015, having surpassed *[Godzilla](Godzilla_(franchise) "Godzilla (franchise)")* as the [highest-grossing film franchise in Japan](List_of_highest-grossing_films_in_Japan "List of highest-grossing films in Japan").[[1]](List_of_Doraemon_films#cite_note-1) As of 2020, the *Doraemon* films have grossed a total of ¥187 billion ($1.7 billion) worldwide.[[2]](List_of_Doraemon_films#cite_note-:31-2) *Doraemon* is the [highest-grossing film in Japan](List_of_highest-grossing_Japanese_films "List of highest-grossing Japanese films") of all time, the [highest-grossing non-English film franchise](List_of_highest-grossing_non-English_films "List of highest-grossing non-English films"), and one of the [highest-grossing animated film franchises](List_of_highest-grossing_animated_films "List of highest-grossing animated films") worldwide.

## Feature films

Most of the original series films were directed by [Tsutomu Shibayama](Tsutomu_Shibayama "Tsutomu Shibayama"). [Shunsuke Kikuchi](Shunsuke_Kikuchi "Shunsuke Kikuchi") was the music and composer of the movies from the year 1980 to 2000, except the 1998 and 1999 movies, whose music was composed by Senri Ohe. Kikuchi was followed by Katsumi Horii for the movies of the years 2000-2004. The music for the films from 2006–17 are composed by [Kan Sawada](Kan_Sawada "Kan Sawada"). [Takayuki Hattori](Takayuki_Hattori "Takayuki Hattori") followed from 2018–present.

Based on my research, I found some information about Doraemon novel adaptations. Here's what I discovered:

## Doraemon Novel Adaptations Found

### 1. **Hideaki Sena's Novel Version (2011)**
- **Title:** *Shōsetsuban Doraemon - Nobita to Tetsujin Heidan* (小説版ドラえもん のび太と鉄人兵団) - "Doraemon Novel Version: Nobita and the Steel Troops"
- **Publisher:** Shogakukan

### 2. **Mizuki Tsujimura's Novel Version (2018)**
- **Title:** Novel version of "Doraemon: Nobita's Chronicle of the Moon Exploration" (のび太の月面探査記)
- **Year:** 2018
- **Author:** Mizuki Tsujimura (award-winning mystery novelist)
- **Note:** Mizuki Tsujimura also wrote the screenplay for this 2019 Doraemon film and is a self-proclaimed Doraemon fan.

## Important Distinction

These are **movie novelizations** (小説版/小説化), not **light novels** (軽小説). There's an important difference:

- **Light novels** (軽小説/ライトノベル): Original prose fiction works with manga-style illustrations, typically originating as new stories
- **Movie novelizations** (小説版): Prose adaptations of existing media (films, in this case)

### Conclusion

**Doraemon does not appear to have independent light novel adaptations.** The novels that exist are primarily **novelizations of the films** published after the movies were released, rather than original light novel series that would have their own independent storylines and illustrations typical of the light novel genre.

The manga (by Fujiko F. Fujio) and anime films remain the primary source material for the franchise, with novels serving as supplementary adaptations rather than original works in the light novel format.

## Naruto Light Novel Adaptations

Naruto has **26 novels** in total, which can be categorized into several types:

### 1. **Film Novelizations (Novelizations)**
From 2002-2015, Shueisha published light novel adaptations of the major Naruto films. The first 7 were written by **Masatoshi Kusakabe**, and some later ones by **Akira Higashiyama** and **Yuka Miyata**:

1. *Naruto: Innocent Heart, Demonic Blood* (Dec 2002) - Licensed in English 2006
2. *Naruto: Mission: Protect the Waterfall Village!* (Dec 2003) - Licensed in English 2007
3. *Naruto: Ninja Clash in the Land of Snow* (Aug 2004)

It was serialized in 's [*shōnen* manga](Sh%C5%8Dnen_manga "Shōnen manga") magazine *[Weekly Shōnen Jump](Weekly_Sh%C5%8Dnen_Jump "Weekly Shōnen Jump")* from October 1990 to June 1996, with the chapters collected into 31 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes. It tells the story of a [basketball](Basketball "Basketball") team from Shōhoku High School in the [Shōnan](Sh%C5%8Dnan "Shōnan") area of Japan. The manga was adapted into an [anime](Anime "Anime") television series by [Toei Animation](Toei_Animation "Toei Animation") which aired from October 1993 to March 1996 and has been broadcast worldwide, enjoying much popularity particularly in Japan, several other Asian countries and Europe. An anime feature film, titled *[The First Slam Dunk](The_First_Slam_Dunk "The First Slam Dunk")*, was released in Japan in December 2022. *Slam Dunk* has 170 million copies in circulation, making it the seventh [best-selling manga series](List_of_best-selling_manga "List of best-selling manga") in history. In 1994, it received the 40th [Shogakukan Manga Award](Shogakukan_Manga_Award "Shogakukan Manga Award") for the *shōnen* category. In 2010, Inoue received special commendations from the [Japan Basketball Association](Japan_Basketball_Association "Japan Basketball Association") for helping popularize [basketball in Japan](Basketball_in_Japan "Basketball in Japan"). ## Plot Further information: [List of *Slam Dunk* characters](List_of_Slam_Dunk_characters "List of Slam Dunk characters") [Hanamichi Sakuragi](Hanamichi_Sakuragi "Hanamichi Sakuragi") is a delinquent and the leader of a gang. He is very unpopular with girls, having been rejected an astonishing fifty times. In his first year at Shohoku High School, Sakuragi meets Haruko Akagi, the girl of his dreams, and is overjoyed when she is not repulsed or scared of him like all the other girls he has asked out. Haruko, recognizing Sakuragi's athleticism, introduces him to the Shohoku basketball team. Sakuragi is reluctant to join the team at first, as he has no prior experience in sports and thinks that basketball is a game for losers because his fiftieth rejection was in favor of a basketball player. Despite his extreme immaturity and fiery temper, he proves to be a natural athlete and joins the team, mainly in the hopes of impressing and getting closer to Haruko. Later on, Sakuragi realizes that he has come to actually love the sport, despite having previously played primarily because of his crush on Haruko. Kaede Rukawa—Sakuragi's bitter rival (both in basketball and because Haruko has a massive crush, albeit one-sided, on Rukawa), the star rookie and a "girl magnet"—joins the team at the same time. Not long after, Hisashi Mitsui, a skilled [three-point](Three-point_shot "Three-point shot") shooter and ex–junior high school [MVP](Most_Valuable_Player "Most Valuable Player"), and Ryota Miyagi, a short but fast [point guard](Point_guard "Point guard"), both rejoin the team and together these four struggle to fulfill team captain Takenori Akagi's dream of winning the national championship. Collectively, these misfits gain publicity and the once little-known Shohoku basketball team becomes an all-star contender in Japan, which gains popularity after defeating one of the powerhouse high school teams at the interhigh championships. ## Production Inoue became inspired to make *Slam Dunk* as he had liked basketball since his high school years. After Inoue started *Slam Dunk*, he was surprised when he began receiving letters from readers that said they started playing the sport due to the manga. His editor even told him "basketball was a taboo in this world." Due to these letters, Inoue decided he wanted to draw better basketball games in the series.[[4]](Slam_Dunk_(manga)#cite_note-4) With the series, Inoue wanted to demonstrate the feelings from some athletes such as their thoughts when they win, lose or improve at their sport. The Japanese [manga](Manga "Manga") series *[Slam Dunk](Slam_Dunk_(manga) "Slam Dunk (manga)")* was written and illustrated by [Takehiko Inoue](Takehiko_Inoue "Takehiko Inoue").[[1]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-slamdunk-1) The story follows [Hanamichi Sakuragi](Hanamichi_Sakuragi "Hanamichi Sakuragi"), who becomes a basketball player from the Shohoku High School basketball team in order to make [Haruko Akagi](Shohoku_High_School_basketball_team "Shohoku High School basketball team"), a girl he likes, fall in love with him. However, as he learns more about basketball and plays several games, he starts liking the sport.

The series was originally published in <Shueisha>'s *[Weekly Shōnen Jump](Weekly_Sh%C5%8Dnen_Jump "Weekly Shōnen Jump")* since the issue 40 from 1990 until the issue 27 from 1996.[[1]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-slamdunk-1)[[2]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-2) The 276 individual chapters were originally collected in 31 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* editions under Shueisha's Jump Comics imprint, with the first volume being published on February 8, 1991[[3]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-SDJPNVolume01-3) and volume 31 on October 3, 1996.[[4]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-SDJPNVolume31-4) It was later reassembled in 24 *[kanzenban](Kanzenban "Kanzenban")* volumes from March 19, 2001[[5]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-5) to February 2, 2002.[[6]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-6) A 20 volume *[shinsōban](Shins%C5%8Dban "Shinsōban")* edition was published between June 1, 2018, and September 1, 2018.[[7]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-7) In 2004, Inoue produced an epilogue titled *Slam Dunk: 10 Days After*, which was drawn on 23 chalkboards in the former campus of the now-defunct Misaki High School located in the [Kanagawa Prefecture](Kanagawa_Prefecture "Kanagawa Prefecture"), which was held for public exhibition from December 3 to December 5. The epilogue, along with coverage of the event, was reprinted in the February 2005 issue of *Switch* magazine.[[1]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-slamdunk-1) [Toei Animation](Toei_Animation "Toei Animation") also adapted the manga into an [anime](Anime "Anime") series which premiered in Japan on October 23, 1993, and ended on March 23, 1996.[[8]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-8)[[9]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-9)

In North America, an English version of *Slam Dunk* was published by the now-defunct [Gutsoon! Entertainment](Gutsoon!_Entertainment "Gutsoon! Entertainment"), which serialized the title in their manga anthology *[Raijin Comics](Raijin_Comics "Raijin Comics")* from 2002 to 2004.[[10]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-10) Five collected volumes were published under Gutsoon's *Raijin Graphic Novels* imprint. They were released from July 2, 2003, until May 5, 2004.[[11]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-SDGTVolume01-11)[[12]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-gutsoonfive-12) After Gutsoon! went out of business, the license for the *Slam Dunk* was purchased by [Viz Media](Viz_Media "Viz Media"), which published a preview of the series in the December 2007 issue of the North American edition of *[Shonen Jump](Shonen_Jump_(magazine) "Shonen Jump (magazine)")*.[[13]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-13)[[14]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-14)[[15]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-15) *Slam Dunk* began serialization in the magazine, starting with the May 2008 issue, as well as in *tankōbon* format with the first being published on September 2, 2008.[[16]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-SDENGVolume01-16)[[17]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-17)[[18]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-18) As of December 3, 2013, Viz has released all thirty-one volumes of the series.[[19]](List_of_Slam_Dunk_chapters#cite_note-SDENGVolume31-19)

The plot consistently evolved with the times and most of the main characters do not really age, despite the fact that the series started in the 1970s and is later clearly set in the 2010s. However, some characters do age, like the grandchild of Buchao, who was a baby in the early volumes, but is now close to junior high, which the author has self-mocked in a few "look back" chapters/episodes. *KochiKame* has a broad audience, ranging from adolescent boys to middle-aged [salarymen](Salaryman "Salaryman"). Ryo-san's antics appeal to children who can laugh at an old buffoon, and to men fearing that they are becoming old buffoons themselves—and also because it often subtly mocks the latest fads and trends. The stories are generally innocent in content, and what little violence appears is comical, while the occasional risqué subjects are included strictly for laughs rather than to titillate. *KochiKame*'s immense popularity has led to guest appearances in the strip by real-life Japanese celebrities such as [Tetsuya Komuro](Tetsuya_Komuro "Tetsuya Komuro").

For creator Osamu Akimoto, *KochiKame* is an homage to the working-class people and districts of old Tokyo, and most chapters open with an elaborate full-page illustration of a <Shitamachi> (downtown) street scene, typically with old wooden buildings and boys playing in the streets.

Based on my research, I can provide you with information about light novel adaptations of KochiKame: Tokyo Beat Cops.

## Light Novel Adaptations of KochiKame

**KochiKame does NOT have traditional light novel adaptations.**

According to the Wikipedia information, KochiKame has been adapted into:
- Anime television series (373 + 27 specials, 1996-2016)
- Three theatrical animated films (by Tatsunoko Production and Studio Gallop)
- Two live-action movies
- Several stage adaptations
- A live-action television series

### The Novelization Anthology

However, there is **one novel-related publication** that featured KochiKame characters:

**"Vs. Kochira Katsushika-ku Kameari Kōen-mae Hashutsujo: Novelization Anthology"** (VS.こち亀 こちらかつしか区亀有公園前派出所ノベライズアンソロジー)

- **Publication Date:** September 17, 2016 (the same day KochiKame's manga ended)
- **Type:** Crossover novelization anthology
- **Content:** Featured KochiKame characters alongside characters from other series including:
  - Girls und Panzer
  - Osomatsu-san
  - Haruchika
  - Cheer Boys!!
  - Sorcerous Stabber Orphen
  - Nazotoki wa Dinner no Ato de

### Conclusion

This anthology was a special crossover publication rather than a dedicated KochiKame light novel adaptation. The KochiKame franchise has primarily been adapted into anime, live-action, and stage formats, but there is no standalone light novel series based on the KochiKame manga itself.

There are **three official light novels** in the Demon Slayer franchise:

"The Gourmet") is a long-running Japanese cooking [manga](Manga "Manga") series written by Tetsu Kariya and drawn by Akira Hanasaki. The manga's title is a [portmanteau](Portmanteau "Portmanteau") of the Japanese word for delicious, *oishii*, and the word for someone who loves to eat, *kuishinbo*.[[3]](Oishinbo#cite_note-Gastronomica-3) The series depicts the adventures of culinary journalist Shirō Yamaoka and his partner (and later wife), Yūko Kurita. Before this suspension, Oishinbo was collected in 111 *[tankōbon](Tank%C5%8Dbon "Tankōbon")* volumes, making it the 10th [longest manga](List_of_manga_series_by_volume_count "List of manga series by volume count") released and the 11th [best-selling manga series](List_of_best-selling_manga "List of best-selling manga") in history. The series was a perennial best-seller, selling 1.2 million copies per volume,[[6]](Oishinbo#cite_note-6) for a total of more than 135 million copies sold.[[7]](Oishinbo#cite_note-7)

The series received the 1986 [Shogakukan Manga Award](Shogakukan_Manga_Award "Shogakukan Manga Award") for [seinen](Seinen "Seinen")/general manga.[[8]](Oishinbo#cite_note-ShogakukanAward-8) It was adapted as a 136-episode [anime](Anime "Anime") television series broadcast on [TV Asahi](TV_Asahi "TV Asahi") from October 17, 1988, to March 17, 1992, followed by two sequel TV anime film specials in 1992 and 1993.

## Plot

Oishinbo is a drama featuring journalist Shirō Yamaoka who works for Tōzai Shimbun. He is a cynical food critic who is tasked by the newspaper's owner, along with the young Yūko Kurita, to provide recipes for the "ultimate menu". During their search, they encounter Yamaoka's fastidious and demanding father, Yūzan Kaibara, a famous gourmand who tries to sabotage Yamaoka's project.

## Characters

The character names listed here are in western order of family name last. The official English language manga volumes use the Japanese naming order of family name first.

Shirō Yamaoka (山岡 士郎, *Yamaoka Shirō*) Voiced by: [Kazuhiko Inoue](Kazuhiko_Inoue "Kazuhiko Inoue")
Played by [Toshiaki Karasawa](Toshiaki_Karasawa "Toshiaki Karasawa") (1994 show), [Masahiro Matsuoka](Masahiro_Matsuoka "Masahiro Matsuoka") (2007 show)

Shirō Yamaoka a 27-year-old journalist for the *Tōzai News* (東西新聞社, *Tōzai Shinbun*)'s culture division and the head of its *Ultimate Menu* project. He is the only son of the world-famous potter and gourmand Yūzan Kaibara. He was forced to cook in his father's *Gourmet Club* when he was still at school and he resents his father, blaming him for his mother's early death. He once destroyed his father's paintings and ceramics because he believed his father cared more about food and his reputation than his family. Yamaoka appears lazy and uninterested unless it concerns food where he possesses a deep knowledge.

Yūko Kurita (栗田 ゆう子, *Kurita Yūko*) Voiced by: [Mayumi Shō](Mayumi_Sh%C5%8D "Mayumi Shō")
Played by [Yuriko Ishida](Yuriko_Ishida "Yuriko Ishida") (1-3), [Yasuko Tomita](Yasuko_Tomita "Yasuko Tomita") (4-5) (1995 show), [Yuka](Y%C5%ABka_(actress) "Yūka (actress)") (2007 show)

Kurita is Yamaoka's co-worker and assists him in the *Ultimate Menu* project. Mantarō Kyōgoku (京極 万太郎, *Kyōgoku Mantarō*) Voiced by: [Takeshi Watabe](Takeshi_Watabe "Takeshi Watabe")
A wealthy businessman and a gourmet who lives in Osaka.

Noriko Hanamura (花村 典子, *Hanamura Noriko*) Voiced by: [Rei Sakuma](Rei_Sakuma "Rei Sakuma")
She is a friend of Yūko Kurita and one of the "Culture Department Flower Trio".

Kinue Tabata (田畑 絹江, *Tabata Kinue*) Voiced by: [Rin Mizuhara](Rin_Mizuhara "Rin Mizuhara")
She is a friend of Yūko Kurita and one of the "Culture Department Flower Trio".

Inspector Nakamatsu (中松警部, *Nakamatsu-keibu*) Voiced by: Norio Fukutome
A Police Inspector with a gruff exterior, but he is quite soft-hearted and forms a friendship with Yamaoka.

Tatsu-san (辰さん) Voiced by: [Reizō Nomoto](Reiz%C5%8D_Nomoto "Reizō Nomoto")
A homeless man who collects leftovers from various restaurants in <Ginza>, so he knows which ones have the highest quality food. He introduced Yamaoka to Okaboshi's restaurant.[[12]](Oishinbo#cite_note-KariyaIzakaya269-12) His full name is Tatsunojō Hanamikōji (花見小路 辰之丈, *Hanamikōji Tatsunojō*).

Tokuo Nakagawa (中川 得夫, *Nakagawa Tokuo*) Voiced by: Ryūji Nakagi
He is the head chef of the *Gourmet Club*.

Kairakutei Black (快楽亭ブラック, *Kairakutei Burakku*) Voiced by: [Takeshi Aono](Takeshi_Aono "Takeshi Aono")
An American food writer and researcher who gets acquainted with Yamaoka and Kurita when he is in Japan studying [tofu](Tofu "Tofu") dishes. He later becomes a [rakugo](Rakugo "Rakugo") artist and takes the name Kairakutei. His original name is Henry James Black but he also uses the [pen name](Pen_name "Pen name") Stan Black.

Terue Yumemi (夢見テルエ, *Yumemi Terue*) Voiced by: [Minami Takayama](Minami_Takayama "Minami Takayama")
One half of a [manzai](Manzai "Manzai") comedy duo. She marries Kairakutei Black and they have a daughter together.

Mariko Niki[[lower-alpha 1]](Oishinbo#cite_note-13) (二木 まり子, *Niki Mariko*) Voiced by: [Saeko Shimazu](Saeko_Shimazu "Saeko Shimazu")
Mariko Niki is a co-worker of Yamaoka and Kurita who writes for Touzai Graph a weekly pictorial magazine. Her family is very wealthy. Her father is Takashi Niki, the president of one of Japan's biggest banks. She studied at a university in Paris and transferred back to Japan from the Touzai Paris office. To the dismay of Yūko Kurita, she pursues Yamaoka romantically but he is not interested in marrying her. Later, she marries a freelance photographer named Kinjō (近城).

Teruko (輝子) Voiced by: [Rihoko Yoshida](Rihoko_Yoshida "Rihoko Yoshida")
Teruko is Mariko's aunt. Mariko believes her difficult personality is the reason she's still unmarried. However, eventually she marries a novelist called Katamori.

Chairman Niki (二木会長, *Niki-kaichō*) Voiced by: [Hisashi Katsuta](Hisashi_Katsuta "Hisashi Katsuta")
Mariko's grandfather and chairman of the Nito Financial Group. He believes he should have a say in who Mariko chooses as a husband.

Arthur Brown (アーサー・ブラウン, *Āsā Buraun*) Voiced by: [Akira Murayama](Akira_Murayama "Akira Murayama")
A friend of Kairakutei Black and an editor for an American magazine. He often asks Yamaoka and his colleagues for help when he writes articles about Japan. His Japanese is strange as he uses archaic words and odd expressions.

### Anime

Main article: [List of Oishinbo episodes](List_of_Oishinbo_episodes "List of Oishinbo episodes")

The manga was adapted into a television anime series that ran from October 1988 to March 1992 for 136 episodes.
The series was followed by two television specials. **Oishinbo: Ultimate VS Supreme** (美味しんぼ 究極対至高 長寿料理対決!!, *Oishinbo: Kyūkyoku Tai Shikō, Chōju Ryōri Taiketsu!!*) was aired in December 1992 and **Oishinbo: Japan-US Rice War** (美味しんぼ 日米コメ戦争, *Oishinbo: Nichibei Kome Sensō*) was aired a year later in December 1993.

## Reception

In the 1980s Japan had an upsurge in popularity in the *gurume* movement, called the "gourmet boom." Iorie Brau, author of "*Oishinbo*’s Adventures in Eating: Food, Communication, and Culture in Japanese Comics," said that this was the largest factor of the increase in popularity of *gurume* comics. The series's first volume sold around one million copies. The popularity of *Oishinbo* the comic lead to the development of the anime, the live action film, and many [fansites](Fansites "Fansites"). The fan-sites chronicle recipes that appeared in the manga.[[3]](Oishinbo#cite_note-Gastronomica-3)

Tetsu Kariya, the writer of *Oishinbo*, said in a 1986 interview that he was not a food connoisseur, and that he felt embarrassed whenever food experts read the comic.[[3]](Oishinbo#cite_note-Gastronomica-3)

## Controversy regarding Fukushima episodes

Responding to severe criticism of Oishinbo's treatment of the Fukushima nuclear disaster, Shogakukan Inc. halted publication of Oishinbo, at least temporarily, its last appearance thus being the May 12, 2014, edition in the weekly Big Comic Spirits.[[5]](Oishinbo#cite_note-ajw.asahi.com-5) Although the halt of publication coincides with the controversy, the editorial staff also claim that it is part of a previously scheduled break.[[37]](Oishinbo#cite_note-38) Before its termination, the final chapters of Oishinbo were given credit with bringing to the forefront a franker discussion of [radiation](Radiation "Radiation") effects flowing from the disaster.[[38]](Oishinbo#cite_note-39)

1. **Manga** (1983-2014) - Original work by Tetsu Kariya and Akira Hanasaki
2. **Anime TV Series** (1988-1992) - 136 episodes
3. **Anime TV Films** (1992, 1993) - Two sequel specials
